original_description: Comprehensive TypeScript/JavaScript coding standards focusing on type safety, defensive programming, and code correctness. Use when (1) Writing or reviewing TS/JS code, (2) Fixing type errors or avoiding any/enum/null, (3) Implementing control flow, state management, or error handling, (4) Applying zero-value pattern or immutability, (5) Code review for TypeScript anti-patterns. Covers naming conventions, function design, return values, bounded iteration, input validation. For performance optimization, use accelint-ts-performance skill. For documentation, use accelint-ts-documentation skill.
best_description: Use this skill for TypeScript/JavaScript code-health work: a review, audit, or refactor whose goal is safer, more predictable, more maintainable code. Invoke it when the user wants a “look over,” “scan,” “clean up,” or best-practices pass on TS/JS modules, helpers, utilities, or packages, or when type errors after a refactor point to weak code patterns rather than framework behavior. It is the right fit for issues around unsafe `any`, weak union narrowing, null/undefined hazards, inconsistent return values, `enum` replacement, `type` vs `interface`, mutation/state handling, loop or control-flow mistakes, incomplete error paths, duplication, naming, and external-input validation. Prefer this skill when the user cares more about correctness and maintainability than speed. Do not use it for performance tuning, tests, security review, docs/JSDoc, or framework-specific debugging.
final_description: Use this skill when the user wants a TypeScript/JavaScript code-quality or best-practices pass: a review, audit, cleanup refactor, or help fixing TS errors that come from weak code patterns. Reach for it when the goal is safer, more predictable, more maintainable code in modules, helpers, utilities, or packages—especially around `any`, union narrowing, null/undefined handling, predictable return values, `enum` vs `as const`, `type` vs `interface`, mutation/state handling, loop or control-flow mistakes, duplication, naming, and incomplete error handling. It is a good fit for “look over this,” “scan for anti-patterns,” “clean this up,” or post-refactor type-safety issues where correctness matters more than speed. Do not use it for performance work, tests, security review, docs/JSDoc, or framework-specific runtime/debugging issues.
